JSON: Name: sim2real_diffusion_adapter Title: Conditional latent diffusion adapter using foundation vision-language models for perceptual sim2real transfer in automated driving Short Hypothesis: At runtime, mapping real-world camera inputs into simulation-conditioned latent representations using a conditional latent diffusion adapter will increase the success rate of simulation-trained behavioral cloning driving policies compared to no adaptation. Related Work: Prior sim2real approaches can be grouped into: (1) domain randomization which trains policies on highly varied synthetic data to force robustness but lacks guarantees of target coverage and requires very large synthetic datasets; (2) image-to-image translation and style-transfer (e.g., CycleGAN variants) which perform offline pixel-level mapping but often introduce artifacts, mode collapse, or semantic shifts and are unstable for diverse open-world inputs; (3) domain adaptation via transfer learning or curriculum learning which refines models with target-domain data but can overfit, requires target samples and retraining of downstream policies, and is sensitive to curriculum design; (4) high-fidelity reconstruction methods (photogrammetry, NeRF, 3D Gaussian splatting) that generate photorealistic environments but incur high data collection and compute costs and do not scale to runtime adaptation; and (5) calibration of dynamics/digital twins which addresses physics gaps but leaves perceptual gaps unresolved. Existing methods therefore trade off data efficiency, modularity, real-time capability, or semantic/geometric consistency; none combine conditional, modular, few-shot, runtime perceptual mapping with foundation vision-language conditioning. Abstract: We address the perceptual simulation-to-reality (sim2real) gap for vision-based automated driving by introducing a conditional latent diffusion adapter that leverages foundation vision-language models as runtime cross-domain translators. The adapter maps incoming real-world camera inputs into simulation-conditioned latent representations using joint image and text conditioning and supports few-shot concept fine-tuning to encode new operational design domains. The framework decouples perception adaptation from downstream autonomy policies, enabling reuse of simulation-trained controllers without retraining. Key contributions are: a conditional latent diffusion runtime adapter that preserves semantic and geometric structure while aligning visual style across domains; a modular few-shot conditioning protocol using concept trigger tokens; and an empirical evaluation protocol assessing perceptual alignment, policy performance, and runtime feasibility on edge and cluster hardware. We expect the adapter to reduce perceptual domain discrepancy and to increase success rates of simulation-trained policies during real-world deployment while remaining computationally tractable for low-speed autonomous platforms. Experiments: Datasets and data collection: 1) Simulation datasets: AutoDRIVE simulator datasets for three digital twin domains: small on-road (racing/figure-8) with 10k-200k frames; large off-road domain with 50k-200k frames. 2) Real-world datasets: Nigel indoor dataset (~1.7k labeled frames, manual laps) and Hunter outdoor dataset (~3.0k labeled frames) collected with different cameras and lighting; additional held-out real scenes for OOD testing (weather, time-of-day, obstacle layouts). 3) Few-shot fine-tuning pools: for each concept, reserve 5 and 10 simulation images for DreamBooth-style fine-tuning. Baselines: A) No adaptation (simulation-trained policy deployed on raw real frames). B) Domain randomization (policy trained on large randomized synthetic dataset; report dataset sizes used). C) CycleGAN-style image translation applied offline to real frames before policy inference. D) Transfer learning: finetune perception or end-to-end policy on small real datasets. Proposed method: conditional latent diffusion adapter with image and text prompts, with and without few-shot fine-tuning. Evaluation metrics: perceptual and statistical alignment - CLIP cosine similarity, CLIP directional score, LPIPS, Gram-style distance (SD) between input/output/style, FID, KID, IS; downstream driving metrics - progress along track (PAT), RMS cross-track error (RMS-XTE), success rate (SR) per trial; runtime metrics - inference iterations-per-second (IPS), end-to-end latency, GPU/CPU memory; statistical tests - paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank (p<0.05) across 10 independent runs. Experimental setup: Train behavioral cloning (BC) policies on simulation-only data (no augmentation) for Nigel and Hunter using identical network architectures. For each test condition run 10 independent real-world trials per condition. Compare policy performance under: (1) no adapter, (2) CycleGAN preprocessed frames, (3) domain-randomized policy, (4) diffusion adapter (no FT), (5) diffusion adapter + 5-shot FT, (6) diffusion adapter + 10-shot FT. Ablations: (A) domain adaptation direction: real2sim vs sim2real conditioning; (B) number of denoising steps {1,5,30}; (C) foundation model variants {SDXL, SDXL-Turbo, SD3M}; (D) input resolution {2560x1096, 640x274}; (E) image-prompt vs text-only conditioning; (F) presence/absence of fine-tuning; (G) measurement of hallucination incidence (frame-level semantic inconsistency rate). Hardware: run training and inference on representative platforms: edge GPU (RTX 2060), desktop GPU (RTX 3080 Ti), and cluster GPUs (V100, A100, H100, L40S); report training time and IPS. Success criteria: statistically significant improvement in SR and reduction in RMS-XTE for diffusion-adapted runs compared to no-adaptation (p<0.05). Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Hallucination and semantic drift: excessive denoising steps or aggressive conditioning can produce hallucinated objects or alter critical scene geometry, causing policy failures. 2) Latency and compute: conditional latent diffusion inference can be compute- and memory-intensive; real-time performance may be infeasible on very constrained hardware or at high camera resolutions. 3) Overfitting in few-shot fine-tuning: DreamBooth-style fine-tuning on very few images may encode spurious correlations and reduce generalization to new scenes. 4) Dependence on foundation models: model licensing, updates, or architecture changes may affect reproducibility and deployment. 5) Limited ODD generalization: adapter may fail to generalize to out-of-distribution real-world conditions (extreme weather, novel textures) not represented by conditioning concepts. 6) Evaluation bias: indoor vs outdoor datasets, camera differences, and limited trial counts can bias measured gains. 7) Safety: runtime adaptation modifies perception stream and may introduce unpredictable failure modes; adapter failures can compromise safety-critical decisions. 8) Scalability: scaling to high-speed driving or multi-sensor fusion (lidar, radar) requires additional development and compute. 9) Reproducibility: variations in prompt engineering, random seeds, and fine-tuning hyperparameters can materially affect results.
